content.text: {"persuasion":"PERSUADED","support_scope":"FULL","rationale":"The BOOK ENTRY's core identification — mountain as a kingdom, nation, or high place, i.e., the seat of ruling authority — is carried directly by the two texts printed with the entry. Jeremiah 51:25 addresses Babylon, an empire, as a 'destroying mountain' that will be made a 'burnt mountain'; the referent is unambiguously an imperial power, not a literal peak and not a place of divine presence. Daniel 2:35 shows the stone becoming a great mountain filling the whole earth, and Daniel 2:44 supplies the inspired interpretation in the same vision: God sets up 'a kingdom which shall never be destroyed.' The supporting chapter adds Revelation 17:9-10, where Scripture itself explicitly equates mountains with kings/kingdoms, and Isaiah 2:2 where the mountain of the LORD's house is exalted above other mountains (kingdom over kingdoms). Every common-interpretation response supplied concedes this kingdom/government sense as a recognized 'common' meaning grounded in these very texts. The strongest counter — mountain as the site of divine presence and revelation (Sinai/Zion) — is a genuine and even dominant sense in other passages, but it cannot account for the entry's own cited texts: Babylon as a destroying mountain cannot be God's dwelling, and the growing mountain of Daniel 2 is interpreted within the text as a kingdom, not a theophany site. A glossary entry is judged against the evidence printed with it, and for that evidence the kingdom reading is not merely defensible but explicitly text-anchored. The secondary elements — 'high place, the seat of ruling authority' and 'Opposite: Valley' — are supported: mountains as lofty seats of exaltation to be brought low is standard (Isa 2:12-14; 40:4), and Isaiah 40:4 pairs mountains made low against valleys exalted, giving the structural opposition the entry asserts. Objections to the chapter's more speculative applications (Rev 8:8, faith moving mountains, the temptation mountain as Babylon the Great) are out of scope for the glossary ruling.","book_core_identification":"A mountain symbolizes a kingdom or nation — a high place functioning as the seat of ruling authority.","book_secondary_elaborations":["The mountain is characterized as a 'high place,' i.e., an exalted seat of power.","The stated symbolic opposite is the valley."],"unsupported_glossary_assertions":[],"chapter_only_objections":["The claim that Revelation 8:8's blazing mountain thrown into the sea must be a world empire depends on the yet-to-be-established 'sea = masses of people' symbol.","Reading Jesus' 'say to this mountain, be removed and cast into the sea' (Matt 17:20; 21:21; Mark 11:23) as referring to Babylon the Great rather than an obstacle/hyperbole is contested and rests on catchphrase composition not defended within this bundle.","Reading 'flee to the mountains' (Matt 24:16) as 'flee to the nations' is strained, since fleeing to literal Judean mountains is the natural sense and the symbolic reading is retrofitted to AD 70 dispersion.","The identification of the 'exceeding high mountain' of the temptation (Matt 4:8) as 'likely Babylon the Great' is speculative.","The claim that valleys represent 'those enslaved by the mountains' goes beyond the printed opposition.","The Joel 2 dawn/mist reading and the Jeremiah 16:16 fishers/hunters application depend on other unestablished symbol chapters."],"strongest_counter_interpretation":"Mountain primarily symbolizes the place of divine presence, revelation, and God's dwelling — Sinai and Zion as the paradigmatic sites of theophany, covenant, and the meeting of heaven and earth (Exod 19-20; Ps 48:1-2; Isa 2:2-3; Matt 17:1-8; Heb 12:18-24).","counter_core_identification":"A mountain is the site of divine encounter and revelation — God's holy dwelling place.","counter_relation_to_book_core":"CONTRADICTS","material_core_denial":"The counter holds that the symbol's referent is a locus of God's presence, not a political power structure; a place of theophany and a human/imperial kingdom cannot both be the core referent of the same symbolic usage in the cited texts.","counter_case":["Sinai and Zion dominate the biblical mountain narrative: covenant law-giving (Exod 19-20), Elijah's encounter (1 Kgs 19), Zion as God's holy hill (Ps 48; Ps 2:6), the Transfiguration (Matt 17), and the Sinai/Zion contrast (Heb 12:18-24).","Standard reference works and mainstream teaching treat divine presence/revelation as the primary symbolic sense, with kingdom/government as a secondary contextual sense.","Even Isaiah 2:2-3 involves the mountain of the LORD's house — a temple/presence motif — so the exaltation-of-Zion texts can be read as presence rather than polity."],"book_explanatory_advantages":["Jeremiah 51:25 explicitly names an empire (Babylon) a 'destroying mountain' — inexplicable on the divine-presence reading, since a wicked destroying power cannot be God's dwelling.","Daniel 2:35 with 2:44 supplies an in-text inspired interpretation: the mountain that fills the earth is God's everlasting kingdom, and the metals it replaces are successive kingdoms.","Revelation 17:9-10 gives Scripture's own explicit equation of mountains with kings/kingdoms, satisfying the book's stated multiple-witness standard (Daniel, Jeremiah, Isaiah, Revelation).","The kingdom reading unifies both positive (God's kingdom, Dan 2; Isa 2:2) and negative (Babylon, Jer 51:25) mountain texts under one referent class — something the divine-presence reading cannot do.","Even Sinai/Zion texts are compatible: Zion as God's mountain is simultaneously the seat of his kingship (Ps 2:6, 'I have set my King on Zion'), so the entry's core does not conflict with the presence motif where God is the ruler enthroned."],"counter_explanatory_advantages":["Better accounts for narrative theophany texts (Sinai, Horeb, Transfiguration) where no political referent is in view.","Reflects the majority emphasis in Christian teaching and reference literature for the term taken across all Scripture."],"evidence_book_core_cannot_explain":[],"comparative_winner":"BOOK","decisive_sources":["Jeremiah 51:25 — Babylon, an empire, expressly called a mountain","Daniel 2:35 with Daniel 2:44 — the mountain interpreted within the text as God's kingdom","Revelation 17:9-10 (cited in supporting chapter) — mountains explicitly identified with kings/kingdoms","Isaiah 2:2 (cited in supporting chapter) — the LORD's mountain exalted above all mountains, i.e., kingdom over kingdoms","Isaiah 40:4 — mountain/valley opposition supporting the printed 'Opposite: Valley'"],"unresolved_objections":["The divine-presence sense remains the more prominent symbolic association for 'mountain' across all Scripture in mainstream teaching; the glossary entry selects the kingdom sense as the definition rather than acknowledging polyvalence — but for the texts the entry actually cites, the kingdom sense is the textually explicit one, so this objection is non-decisive for the entry as printed."],"confidence":"high"}
